strengths: Clear problem identification and strong empirical motivation for entropy collapse in RLVR training through controlled experiments (Figure 2)
Elegant and intuitive solution design with thoughtful details (e.g., reward-shaping to prevent trivial problem synthesis)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 model sizes and 12+ benchmarks with substantial improvements on competition-level benchmarks (18.3% and 22.8% gains on AIME24/25 Pass@32)
Convincing analysis of entropy maintenance (Figure 5) and Pass@k scaling behavior that demonstrates reasoning boundary expansion
Well-written paper with clear presentation, informative visualizations (especially Figure 4), and detailed algorithms
Algorithm-agnostic framework applicable to multiple RLVR methods (PPO, GSPO, Reinforce++)
Consistent improvements across all model sizes and datasets, suggesting good generalizability
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core insight (data diversity maintains exploration) is relatively straightforward; problem synthesis from correct solutions is intuitive but not deeply novel; related work (SwS) also proposes problem synthesis with similar core ideas
Reward-shaping design (Eq. 6) with dual accuracy thresholds [12.5%-50%] and [12.5%-62.5%] appears ad-hoc with no ablation studies or sensitivity analysis justifying these specific ranges

Unvalidated core assumption: paper claims synthetic problems preserve original answers but provides no empirical verification; only Figure 4 examples are shown; no quantitative measurement of semantic similarity between original and synthetic problems
Missing computational cost analysis: method requires additional forward/backward passes for synthesis and synthetic problem solving, but training overhead is never discussed or quantified

Insufficient ablation studies: no systematic ablations separating entropy maintenance from other contributing factors (problem diversity, additional training signals); causality not rigorously established
Inconsistent results on some benchmarks: negative gains on OlymE (-3.7%) and OlymH (-1.6%) with DAPO-17k; solution of mixing in DeepMath data appears ad-hoc and suggests potential overfitting

Limited comparison with alternative augmentation strategies: mentions MetaMath rephrasing but provides only preliminary comparison; no systematic comparison with other recent data augmentation methods for RLVR
Missing implementation details: hyperparameter selection process unexplained; unclear if thresholds require per-domain tuning; code availability not mentioned
Prompt engineering sensitivity not discussed: Figure 8 shows detailed synthesis prompt, but sensitivity to prompt design and potential for prompt-specific results not addressed
Limited novelty in general-domain transfer: Table 3 shows only modest improvements (1-2 points) on general QA tasks, suggesting method is specialized to mathematical reasoning

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 12 benchmarks, multiple model sizes (3B-32B), and multiple datasets

Thorough analysis sections including policy entropy trajectories (Figure 5), Pass@k scaling (Figure 6), and transfer to general tasks

weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: problem augmentation for data synthesis is well-established; SVS is an incremental application to RLVR without clear conceptual advance

No confidence intervals or significance tests reported; high variance visible in figures raises reliability concerns for some reported improvements

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear empirical evidence of entropy collapse in RLVR (Figure 2). Strong connection established between data diversity and policy entropy.
Substantial and consistent empirical improvements: 18.3%-22.8% gains on AIME Pass@32, 2-3% average across 12 benchmarks, consistent across model sizes (3B-32B).
Comprehensive experimental validation: 12 diverse benchmarks, proper ablations (Section 5.3), entropy trajectory analysis, Pass@k scaling to k=1024, and generalization to code generation.
Well-designed technical approach: clever reward shaping (Eq. 4) prevents trivial problems, clear algorithm specification, proper GRPO data filtering, algorithm agnostic to optimizer choice.
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, full prompts, extensive appendices with case studies, clear implementation details for replication.
Strong analytical work: demonstrates entropy maintenance mechanism (Figure 5), pushes reasoning boundaries beyond base model (Figure 6), multiple alternative augmentation strategies tested.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is incremental application of well-known techniques (online data augmentation + self-play) to RLVR. Insufficient differentiation from concurrent SwS (Liang et al., 2025) which uses similar model-generated augmentation.

Synthetic problem quality concerns: only ~80% of synthetic problems judged valid by SOTA LLMs (Figure 13), with validity decreasing over training. While authors argue manually-checked problems remain solvable, inherent uncertainty about training on potentially flawed problems persists.

Insufficient theoretical grounding: no formal analysis of why preserving problem semantics improves exploration beyond 'more data.' Missing connection to curriculum learning or information-theoretic frameworks. Mechanism in Section E.2 is under-explored.

Hyperparameter choices under-justified: accuracy ranges [0.125, 0.5] and [0.125, 0.625] appear arbitrary with no ablation studies. Hard thresholds in Eq. 4 vs. softer alternatives unexplored. Sensitivity analysis missing.

Computational cost-benefit unclear: Section 5.5 shows overhead but limited discussion of tradeoffs. On DAPO-17k, early stages have high synthetic generation volume. On MATH-12k (80% initial accuracy), gains are marginal. Missing wall-clock time comparisons.

Performance degradation on open-ended answers: substantial drops on OlymH (-1.8%) and AGIEval (small but consistent) with DAPO-17k, indicating overfitting to integer-answer format. Limited analysis of when/why format bias emerges.

Statistical rigor gaps: no error bars or confidence intervals in main results (Tables 1-2) despite visible variance in intermediate evaluation plots. Unclear whether all improvements are statistically significant.
Limited failure analysis: no characterization of problem types where SvS struggles, categories where synthetic problems hurt, or conditions where standard RLVR is preferable.

strengths: Well-motivated problem with convincing empirical diagnosis: identifies and clearly demonstrates entropy collapse in standard RLVR limits Pass@k improvement (Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 reasoning benchmarks, models from 3B-32B, both Pass@1 and Pass@k metrics including high-k evaluation (k=1024), code generation extension
Consistent improvements across settings with particularly strong results on competition-level benchmarks (18.3-22.8% Pass@32 gains on AIME 24/25)
Direct empirical evidence that data diversity preserves policy entropy: Figure 5 clearly shows SvS maintains stable entropy while baseline collapses
Thoughtful ablation studies distinguishing between 'more training data', 'harder problems', and 'synthesized problems' components

Honest analysis of limitations: acknowledges only ~80% synthetic problem validity (E.5), reveals format-specific overfitting requiring additional data augmentation, provides computational cost transparency (5.5)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution (generating variational problems from correct solutions) is incremental over existing problem augmentation approaches; closely related SwS method (Liang et al., 2025) not directly compared

Questionable synthetic problem quality and technical soundness: only ~80% synthetic problems deemed valid by SOTA LLMs (E.5); Figure 4 explicitly shows failed synthesis cases; verification mechanism is circular (Eq. 2) using original problem's answer rather than validating semantic correctness

Ad-hoc hyperparameter choices without principled justification: hardcoded accuracy ranges [12.5%-50%] and [12.5%-62.5%] lack sensitivity analysis or principled derivation; unclear how to set for new tasks or problem types

Weak experimental comparisons: primary baseline is vanilla RLVR only; critical comparison with SwS missing; related entropy regularization methods (Clip-Cov) relegated to appendix; confounded variables across settings (different training steps, data formats)

Generalization concerns and format overfitting: substantial performance drops on non-integer benchmarks when trained on DAPO-17k (Table 2); requires additional DeepMath data to restore performance, suggesting model overfits to problem format rather than learning robust reasoning

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: doesn't explain why variational problems specifically preserve entropy better than simply having more diverse problems; circular dependency - why doesn't model memorize synthetic-original problem mapping?

Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; given sampling variance, some reported improvements within noise (especially for smaller models); reproducibility limited by no code release

Presentation and clarity issues: key technical details scattered across appendices; dense paper with case studies taking excessive space (Appendix J); connection between entropy and data diversity not clearly explained upfront

strengths: Clear motivation addressing real entropy collapse problem in RLVR with compelling preliminary evidence (Figure 2)
Elegant, practical approach using policy-generated solutions to create synthetic problems with guaranteed valid answers

Strong empirical results on challenging benchmarks (18.3%-22.8% Pass@32 improvements on AIME 24/25)

High variance in results without confidence intervals or statistical significance testing; some Pass@1 improvements marginal
